narrative: The model estimates a 19% chance that you will fail the final year. That means roughly one in five students with a similar profile would not pass; it is not a certainty, but it is enough for the school to require remedial courses as preventive support. The strongest influences on this decision are actually protective. Your history of past class failures is the top-ranked factor, and because you have none, it strongly lowers your risk. Your intention to pursue higher education is next, and wanting to continue studying also works in your favor. The third factor, how often you go out with friends, is at a medium level; this is the most common pattern among students who passed, so it does not raise the warning and slightly favors passing. Because these leading signals lean toward passing, the 19% flag comes from smaller concerns adding up—such as no internet at home, very long travel to school, and some less common family-job patterns—rather than from the top three. To improve, use the remedial courses to establish a steady weekly study routine, attend every class, ask for help early in difficult subjects, and protect study time around travel and social activities.
